reclassified: 'Fragrance' was historically treated as one harmless scent note; undisclosed blends routinely contain phthalates & synthetic musks — endocrine/repro flags (Prop 65 phthalates) and contact allergens.
Fragrance.note: Undisclosed blend. Hazards assigned from documented fragrance-carrier chemistry (phthalates, musks), not the specific formula.

reclassified: MIT was the 'safe' preservative replacing parabens; became 2013 'Allergen of the Year' — epidemic of allergic contact dermatitis, now restricted in leave-on products (EU).

Propylene Glycol.note: Low acute hazard; mild skin irritant at high concentration.

Enzymes.s: Biological catalysts, may cause respiratory sensitization
reclassified: Enzymes were added to laundry products as 'natural' boosters; they are potent respiratory sensitizers — industry adopted encapsulation after occupational asthma outbreaks (1970s).
Enzymes.note: Encapsulated in modern products to reduce aerosolization.

Sodium Chloride.s: Table salt, no hazard in cleaning context

Alumina.s: Natural abrasive, low hazard in cleaning paste form

Brassica Campestris Seed Oil.s: Field mustard seed oil, natural emollient

reclassified: Ethanol was long marketed as a harmless 'natural' solvent; high-exposure studies documented fetal harm (FAS), and occupational exposure is now treated more cautiously.

Sodium Hypochlorite.s: Corrosive, severe eye damage, aquatic toxicity
reclassified: Bleach was the unquestioned household standard for a century; occupational cohorts (cleaning workers, nurses) later linked routine bleach exposure to asthma & COPD risk.

Quaternary Ammonium.s: Harmful if swallowed, corrosive, aquatic toxicity
reclassified: Quats surged as 'safe' germ killers; occupational studies linked them to asthma & allergic sensitization; EPA registration review ongoing.

Benzalkonium Chloride.s: Harmful if swallowed, corrosive, aquatic toxicity
reclassified: Benzalkonium chloride was a go-to 'mild' disinfectant; animal repro studies + occupational asthma reports led to stricter limits & allergy labeling.
SLS was once marketed as 'safe enough to brush your teeth with'; stripping studies & 1,4-dioxane contamination concerns (from ethoxylation variants) later tempered that.
SLES replaced SLS as 'gentler'; ethoxylation introduces trace 1,4-dioxane (IARC 2B probable carcinogen) — a contaminant, not an ingredient.

Limonene.s: Flammable, skin sensitizer, aspiration hazard, aquatic toxicity
reclassified: Citrus limonene was sold as the 'natural' scent; on air exposure it oxidizes into potent sensitizers (limonene hydroperoxides) — now a known contact-allergen source.

Sodium Percarbonate.s: Oxidizer, harmful if swallowed, severe eye damage

Tea Tree Oil.s: Skin sensitizer, aspiration hazard, respiratory irritant
reclassified: Tea tree oil rode the 'natural = safe' wave; it is a documented contact sensitizer (oxidized forms) and has rare prepubertal gynecomastia case reports (weak endocrine signal).
Lavender oil, once 'calming & innocent', has case reports linking topical use to prepubertal gynecomastia (weak, possible endocrine activity); a registered contact allergen.

Eucalyptus Oil.s: Skin sensitizer, respiratory irritant, toxic to pets

reclassified: CAPB replaced harsher surfactants as 'gentle'; became a common contact allergen (amide impurities) — now on many allergen patch panels.

Benzisothiazolinone.s: Harmful if swallowed, skin irritant, aquatic toxicity
reclassified: BIT, a cousin of MIT, followed the same arc: marketed safe, became a recognized sensitizer with occupational dermatitis reports.
Phenoxyethanol replaced parabens as 'clean' preservative; repro/developmental flags in animal studies led to EU restrictions in cosmetics (2012).
2-Butoxyethanol (EGBE) was once in every window & all-purpose cleaner as a 'safe' solvent; CA Prop 65 lists it for reproductive/developmental harm; EPA risk reviews followed.
Ammonia was grandma's go-to; strong respiratory irritant, and mixing with bleach produces chloramine gas — a documented household emergency.
Ethoxylated surfactants can carry trace 1,4-dioxane (IARC 2B probable carcinogen) from manufacturing — process contaminant, not on the label.

Sodium Carbonate Peroxide.s: Oxidizer, harmful if swallowed, severe eye damage

Potassium Oleate.s: Potassium salt of oleic acid, mild irritant

Essential Oils.s: May cause skin sensitization. Varies by oil type.
Essential Oils.note: Varies widely by oil; sensitization is the common thread.

Citrus essential oils.s: May cause skin sensitization. Contains limonene.

Potassium Hydroxide.s: Corrosive in pure form, but neutralized in final product
Potassium Hydroxide.note: Corrosive in pure form; neutralized in finished products.

Potassium Carbonate.s: Mild alkali, can cause skin/eye irritation in pure form

Dipterocarpus Wood Oil.s: Natural essential oil, may cause sensitization

Citral.s: Fragrance allergen, occurs naturally in citrus oils

Mandarin Oil.s: Citrus essential oil, may cause sensitization

Denatured Alcohol.s: Ethanol denatured with bitterants, flammable, eye irritant
reclassified: Denatured alcohol is ethanol + bitterants; inherits ethanol's high-exposure repro flags. Often the hidden volatile in 'natural' spray cleaners.

Citrus Aurantium Peel Oil.s: Bitter orange peel oil, may cause sensitization

Ethanolamine.s: Corrosive amine. Occupational asthma documented in cleaners (meta-analyses).

Surfactant.s: Undisclosed surfactant blend — cannot assess specific hazards.
Surfactant.note: Undisclosed blend; generic placeholder used when the true surfactant is unknown.

Dimethicone.s: Silicone polymer. Low hazard, persistent in environment.
Dimethicone.note: Not acutely toxic but poorly biodegradable; accumulates.

Butane.s: Extremely flammable propellant gas. Simple asphyxiant in confined spaces.

Hydrogen Peroxide.s: Corrosive oxidizer. Severe eye damage, aquatic toxicity.

Hydroxypropyl Cyclodextrin.s: Modified starch ring that traps odor molecules. Low hazard.

Alcohol.s: Generic alcohol (usually ethanol or isopropanol). Flammable, eye irritant.

Propane.s: Extremely flammable propellant gas. Simple asphyxiant in confined spaces.

Propylene Glycol Butyl Ether.s: Glycol ether solvent. Repro/developmental concern (glycol ether class, EPA/Prop 65 flagged 2-butoxyethanol cousin).
reclassified: Glycol ethers were promoted as 'safe' replacements for banned solvents (1970s–90s); regulation & Prop 65 listings later flagged reproductive/developmental harm in the class.

Sodium Dodecylbenzenesulfonate.s: Anionic surfactant (linear alkylbenzene sulfonate). Skin/eye irritant, aquatic toxicity.

Alcohol Ethoxylates.s: Ethoxylated surfactant family. Skin/eye irritant; 1,4-dioxane contaminant trace concern from ethoxylation.
reclassified: Ethoxylated surfactants (SLES, alcohol ethoxylates) can carry trace 1,4-dioxane — a byproduct EPA flagged as a probable human carcinogen (IARC 2B). Not an added ingredient; a process contaminant.

Didecyldimonium Chloride.s: Quaternary ammonium (DDAC). Corrosive, aquatic toxicity, respiratory sensitizer in occupational use.
reclassified: Quats (quaternary ammonium disinfectants) surged in use mid-20th c. as 'safe' germ killers; occupational studies later linked them to asthma & allergic sensitization.

Isoparaffin.s: Petroleum-derived solvent blend. Flammable, aspiration hazard.

Phenoxyisopropanol.s: Glycol ether-like solvent. Skin/eye irritant; glycol ether class repro flags.

Isobutane.s: Extremely flammable propellant gas. Simple asphyxiant in confined spaces.

Sodium Silicate.s: Alkaline silicate. Corrosive; dust respiratory irritant.

Sodium Tetraborate.s: Borax (sodium tetraborate decahydrate). EU/CLP-classified reproductive toxicant 1B (H360FD); eye irritant. US allows in household products.
reclassified: Borax was the 19th-century 'miracle cleaner' — cheap, effective, universally trusted. EU CLP classified it Reproductive toxicant 1B (H360FD) in 2010; it is restricted across Europe while the US still sells it off the shelf.
Sodium Tetraborate.note: The catch-up poster child: identical GHS hazard classification on both sides of the Atlantic, opposite regulatory outcomes.

Diethylene Glycol Monobutyl Ether.s: DEGBE — glycol ether solvent used in heavy-duty oven and floor cleaners. Harmful if swallowed, eye irritant. Glycol-ether class carries reproductive/developmental concern in EU/Prop 65 classifications.
reclassified: DEGBE is a glycol ether — the same family as 2-butoxyethanol (EGBE). Glycol ethers were adopted as 'safer' replacements for banned solvents through the 1980s-90s; EU CLP later flagged reproductive/developmental toxicity across the class and several are now CA Prop 65-listed. Lower acute toxicity than EGBE, but the class concern stands.
Diethylene Glycol Monobutyl Ether.note: Common in fume-style oven cleaners where high heat vaporizes the solvent.
